q: What systolic blood pressure drop defines the orthostatic component of MSA diagnostic criteria?
o: A rise in systolic blood pressure
A 30 mm Hg drop in systolic blood pressure
A 20 mm Hg drop in systolic blood pressure
A 10 mm Hg drop in diastolic blood pressure
explanation:
The orthostatic component of MSA diagnostic criteria requires a 30 mm Hg systolic blood-pressure drop (p986).

C. A 20 mm Hg drop in systolic blood pressure: This is a practical significance threshold, contrasted with the MSA diagnostic criterion (p986); the requested value is a 30 mm Hg drop in systolic blood pressure (p986).
D. A 10 mm Hg drop in diastolic blood pressure: This is the practical diastolic threshold, not the requested systolic criterion (p986); the requested value is a 30 mm Hg drop in systolic blood pressure (p986).
A. A rise in systolic blood pressure: The criterion requires a drop, not a rise (p986); the requested value is a 30 mm Hg drop in systolic blood pressure (p986).

q: What characteristic, though nonspecific, MRI sign is described in the pons in MSA?
o: Slit-like marginal hypointensity lateral to the putamen
explanation:
MSA can produce a characteristic but nonspecific hot cross bun sign in the pons and middle cerebellar peduncles (p986).

D. Slit-like marginal hypointensity lateral to the putamen: This is a putaminal finding, not the described pontine sign (p986).
B. Frontotemporal atrophy: This supports probable bvFTD, not the pontine MSA sign (p982).
C. Cortical microbleeds from amyloid angiopathy: These belong to the cortical hemorrhage discussion, not the MSA pontine sign (p994).

q: How many of the six possible bvFTD symptoms are required to meet "possible" bvFTD criteria?
explanation:
Possible bvFTD criteria require three of the six specified symptoms (p982).

D. Six: Six is the number of listed possible symptoms, not the number required (p982); the requested value is three (p982).
C. Five: Five is the upper end of annual MMSE decline in DLB, not the bvFTD symptom count (p984); the requested value is three (p982).
A. Four: Four is the lower end of annual MMSE decline in DLB, not the bvFTD symptom count (p984); the requested value is three (p982).

q: What fraction of all FTD cases does bvFTD account for?
explanation:
In most centers, bvFTD accounts for more than 50% of all FTD cases (p987).

D. Less than 10%: This is the share with FUS protein aggregates, not the bvFTD clinical share (p987); the requested value is more than 50% (p987).
C. Approximately 20%: This is nfvPPA with TDP pathology (p988); the requested value is more than 50% (p987).
B. 15%: This is RBD prevalence in Parkinson disease (p983); the requested value is more than 50% (p987).

q: What TDP-43 subtype is typically seen at autopsy in svPPA?
explanation:
Patients with svPPA often have TDP-43 type C-positive, tau-negative inclusions at autopsy (p988).

D. TDP-43 type A: This is the usual TDP subtype in the TDP-positive minority of nfvPPA cases (p988).
A. TDP-43 type B: This is associated with motor neuron disease and often C9orf72 FTD-ALS (p990).
B. TDP-43 type D: This is seen with the rare valosin mutation (p990).

q: What gene mutation, discovered in 2011, is the major cause of familial FTD, ALS, and FTD-ALS?
explanation:
A C9orf72 mutation discovered in 2011 is a major cause of familial FTD, ALS and FTD-ALS (p990).

D. MAPT: MAPT was identified in 1998 for FTDP-17; it is not the 2011 FTD/ALS discovery (p990).
B. Progranulin: The book assigns progranulin mutations to TDP type A; the specified 2011 discovery is C9orf72 (p990).
A. Valosin: This rare FTD mutation is associated with TDP type D, not the specified major FTD-ALS discovery (p990).

q: Which FDA-approved drug extends survival and delays the need for ventilation in ALS?
explanation:
Riluzole extends survival and delays the need for ventilatory support in ALS (p991).

D. Levodopa: The book uses levodopa for parkinsonian symptoms in DLB after stabilization, not ALS survival (p984; p991).
B. Cholinesterase inhibitors: These are tried for DLB cognition/hallucinations, not the stated ALS survival effect (p984; p991).
C. Anticholinergic medications: DLB patients are advised to avoid these; the ALS survival drug named is riluzole (p984; p991).

q: In what percentage of PSP cases do falls occur as the first manifestation of disease?
explanation:
Falls are the first manifestation in 60% of PSP cases in the description cited (p992).

D. 46%: This is dysphagia during the first five years of PSP (p992); the requested value is 60% (p992).
B. About a quarter: This is bradykinesia in autopsy-proven PSP cases (p992); the requested value is 60% (p992).
A. 85%: This is RBD prevalence in DLB (p983); the requested value is 60% (p992).

q: In an older adult with a new cortical (lobar) hemorrhage, what diagnosis should be suspected instead of hypertension?
o: Hypertension as the typical explanation for cortical hemorrhage
explanation:
Cortical hemorrhages commonly occur with cerebral amyloid angiopathy, whereas hypertension characteristically produces hemorrhage in deep structures (p994).

D. Hypertension as the typical explanation for cortical hemorrhage: The book contrasts deep hypertensive hemorrhages with cortical CAA hemorrhages (p994).
A. Multiple system atrophy: Its described diagnostic features include autonomic failure and pontocerebellar changes; cortical amyloid hemorrhage is attributed to CAA (p986; p994).
B. Progressive supranuclear palsy: PSP is characterized by vertical gaze palsy and early gait/fall features; this cortical hemorrhage clue is assigned to CAA (p992; p994).
